---
name: fathom-custodian
description: >
  Register falsifiable concerns about a repo's agent configuration
  (CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md) and act on `fathom config audit` violations —
  the "instructed means true" loop, where fathom is the instrument and
  THIS session is the hand. Use when config feels stale, after a doctor
  `concerns` failure or a session-start config attention line, when asked
  to "keep CLAUDE.md honest", or to set up config contracts in a newly
  wired repo.

<!-- fathom:owned — generated by `fathom init --skills`; safe to delete this line to adopt the file as your own -->

Agent config is a pile of claims about a codebase, and codebases move —
so config rots into *confident misdirection*: an agent believes its
config harder than it believes the code. The custodian audits registered
**concerns** (falsifiable wants) against reality. The division of labor
is absolute and is the reason this can run continuously: **fathom
reports; it never edits your prose.** You — the session, with context and
a human present — decide what to change.

## 1. Read the audit

```sh
fathom config audit [--repo .] [--json]
```

Per concern: `✓ holds` (with what was checked), `✗ violated` (evidence as
`file:line`, plus the concern's `want`/`why`), `~ unable to check`
(reason — never a silent skip), `– off` (a disabled inherited concern,
named rather than hidden). Exit `1` iff anything is violated. Zero
concerns registered exits `0` with the absence named — normal, not
broken.

## 2. Register concerns (`.fathom/concerns.cue` — this repo governs; `~/.fathom/concerns.cue` — your defaults everywhere)

```cue
concerns: {
	deploy_safety: {
		want:  "no raw-copy deploy instruction anywhere in agent config"
		why:   "an unsigned binary copied over the running daemon once took it down fleet-wide"
		check: {kind: "forbidden_pattern", pattern: "cp .*libexec/fathom"}
	}
	gate_documented: {
		want:  "the deterministic gate is named in agent config and its target exists"
		check: {kind: "command_documented_and_exists", command: "task validate"}
	}
	router_thin: {check: {kind: "max_lines", file: "CLAUDE.md", lines: 120}, want: "the root CLAUDE.md stays a router"}
	pointers_hold: {check: {kind: "pointers_resolve"}, want: "every pointer in agent config resolves"}
}
```

Rules the loader enforces (loudly, all errors at once): a concern without
a machine-evaluable `check` is refused — an uncheckable concern is a
wish; unknown check kinds are refused by name; `field?:` (CUE optional)
is refused because in a config instance it sets nothing while looking
like it does. A project entry with the same name replaces the user entry
wholesale; `off: true` disables an inherited concern (still shown).
Authoring bar: 2–4 concerns whose `why` names a mistake that actually
happened — speculative contracts teach people to ignore the audit.

The four v1 check kinds: `forbidden_pattern` (regexp over agent-config
files, `file:line` evidence), `command_documented_and_exists` (the
instruction-outlives-the-command failure, both halves named), `max_lines`
(router thinness), `pointers_resolve` (markdown links AND backtick repo
paths, precision-guarded so foreign names — Go modules, kit packages —
are never flagged).

## 3. Act on a violation — you are the hand

1. Read the evidence (`file:line`) and decide which is wrong: the config
   (usually — update the instruction to match reality) or the world (a
   promised dir/target that should exist — create it).
2. Make the edit yourself, in this session. Never expect fathom to fix
   prose, and never suppress a violation by deleting the concern without
   saying so — `off: true` in the repo scope is the honest disable, and
   the audit will keep naming it.
3. Re-run `fathom config audit` and show holds. A violation you fixed is
   worth one line in the commit message: config rot caught by contract.

## 4. Where else it surfaces

- `fathom doctor` has a `concerns` row (red only for a load error or a
  violation; zero concerns is a passing row naming the absence).
- Session start (Claude Code, `startup`/`clear` only) injects one
  attention line while violations exist — its whole delivery is calling
  attention; it edits nothing.
- File friction with the checks themselves (a false violation, a
  vacuous hold) via the `fathom-feedback` skill — precision failures
  teach people to ignore the custodian, so they are P1 bugs, not nits.
